discount-calculator.assumptionNote: Assumes discounts apply sequentially to the reduced price and tax applies to the final discounted price.
benefits: Exposes the real price behind 'was/now' marketing.
Shows stacked coupons' true combined effect.
Prevents mental-math errors at the checkout.
Makes comparing two sale offers instant.

faqs.a: Because the second discount applies to the already-discounted price, not the original. 25% off ₹2,000 leaves ₹1,500; 10% off that leaves ₹1,350. Total saved is ₹650, which is 32.5% of ₹2,000. Stacked discounts always multiply: (1−0.25)×(1−0.10) = 0.675, so you pay 67.5%.
Divide the sale price by (1 − discount/100). A ₹1,350 item at 32.5% off was originally 1,350 / 0.675 = ₹2,000. Handy for checking whether a 'was' price on the tag is honest.
faqs.q: How do I reverse-calculate the original price?

faqs.a: After, in almost every jurisdiction — you pay tax on what you actually pay. That is why the calculator applies tax to the discounted price. If a store ever taxes the pre-discount price, that is worth questioning.
faqs.q: Is tax charged before or after the discount?

faqs.a: A discount lowers the price you pay now; cashback returns money later (often as store credit or after conditions). A 10% discount beats 10% cashback because the cashback may expire, be restricted, or require another purchase.
faqs.q: What's the difference between discount and cashback?

faqs.a: BOGO on identical items equals 50% off per item — better than most percent sales. But it forces you to buy two. If you only needed one, a 30% discount on a single item is the better deal for you.
faqs.q: How do I compare 'buy 1 get 1 free' with a percent discount?

faqs.a: Often. 'Was ₹4,000, now ₹2,000' only means something if the item actually sold at ₹4,000. Retailers inflate was-prices before sales. Track the price for a few weeks before big sale events, or compare with other stores.
faqs.q: Do sale prices include hidden markups?

discount-calculator.formula:
Discount amount = price x discount% / 100.
Sale price = price - discount amount.
Stacked: final = price x (1 - d1/100) x (1 - d2/100).
Effective discount = (price - final) / price x 100.
howTo: Add an extra coupon discount if you have one (0 if not).
Add tax if needed, then read the sale price and your savings.
keyFacts: Discounts apply to the current price — stacked discounts multiply, they don't add.
25% off followed by 10% off equals 32.5% off, not 35%.
Tax is charged on the discounted price, not the original — a small extra saving.
'Up to 70% off' usually means one item; the average discount is far lower.
A discount only saves money if you were going to buy it anyway.

discount-calculator.quickAnswer: A ₹2,000 item at 25% off costs ₹1,500. Stack an extra 10% coupon and it drops to ₹1,350 — you save ₹650 total, an effective 32.5% off. Note the trick: 25% + 10% is not 35% off, because the second discount applies to the already-reduced price.
